## Big idea in one line

**Do not expose your database entity as the API contract.**  
Use a **DTO** (Data Transfer Object) for what goes in/out of the HTTP layer, and **validate** that DTO before your service runs.

```text
Client JSON
    │
    ▼
Request DTO  (+ @Valid rules)
    │
    ▼
Service maps DTO ↔ Entity
    │
    ▼
DB / Entity
    │
    ▼
Response DTO → JSON to client
```

***

## Why DTOs? (plain problem)

If the controller accepts the **Entity** directly:

| Risk | What goes wrong |
|------|-----------------|
| Extra fields | Client can send `id`, `role`, `createdAt` and overwrite things |
| Leakage | Response may show password hashes, internal flags, relations |
| Coupling | Changing DB columns instantly changes your public API |

**DTO fix:** the API shape is a separate class. The entity stays an internal detail.

***

## Topic 1 — Request DTO vs Response DTO

Often you want **two** shapes:

```text
CreateUserRequest   → name, email, password   (input only)
UserResponse        → id, name, email         (no password)
```

Same idea for Product, Order, etc.

### Simple class style

```java
public class CreateUserRequest {
    private String name;
    private String email;
    private String password;

    // getters + setters (or Lombok @Data / @Getter @Setter)
}
```

```java
public class UserResponse {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;

    public UserResponse(Long id, String name, String email) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
    }

    // getters
}
```

### Record style (clean for immutable DTOs)

```java
public record CreateUserRequest(String name, String email, String password) {}
public record UserResponse(Long id, String name, String email) {}
```

Use whatever your project already uses. Records are short; classes are fine too.

***

## Topic 2 — Map Entity ↔ DTO (no magic required)

In the service (or a small mapper helper):

```java
private UserResponse toResponse(User user) {
    return new UserResponse(user.getId(), user.getName(), user.getEmail());
}

private User toEntity(CreateUserRequest req) {
    User user = new User();
    user.setName(req.name());
    user.setEmail(req.email());
    user.setPassword(req.password()); // later: hash this
    return user;
}
```

Controller stays thin:

```java
@PostMapping("/users")
public UserResponse create(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
    return userService.create(request);
}
```

***

## Topic 3 — Bean Validation (why + dependency)

**Problem:** empty email, blank name, bad password length.  
You do **not** want `if` soup in every controller.

**Fix:** annotate DTO fields + tell Spring to check them.

### Dependency

Add **Validation** on [start.spring.io](https://start.spring.io/) or in `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Common annotations:

| Annotation | Plain meaning |
|------------|---------------|
| `@NotNull` | value must not be null |
| `@NotBlank` | string not null/empty/whitespace |
| `@NotEmpty` | collection/string not empty |
| `@Email` | looks like an email |
| `@Size(min, max)` | length / collection size |
| `@Min` / `@Max` | number bounds |
| `@Positive` | number > 0 |
| `@Pattern(regexp=...)` | custom format |

***

## Topic 4 — Wire validation on the controller

Annotate the DTO:

```java
public record CreateUserRequest(
    @NotBlank String name,
    @NotBlank @Email String email,
    @NotBlank @Size(min = 8, max = 64) String password
) {}
```

Put **`@Valid`** (or `@Validated`) on the controller parameter:

```java
@PostMapping("/users")
public UserResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
    return userService.create(request);
}
```

```text
JSON arrives
  → Jackson builds CreateUserRequest
  → @Valid runs Bean Validation
  → if fail: MethodArgumentNotValidException (400 by default path)
  → if ok: method body runs
```

**Forgot `@Valid`?** Annotations on the DTO do nothing. This is the #1 beginner bug.

## Practice lab (IDE steps)

### Step 1 — Project

1. Open your existing Boot Web + JPA product/user app (or a tiny new one from Initializr: Web + Validation + H2/JPA).
2. Confirm `spring-boot-starter-validation` is in the POM.

### Step 2 — Create DTO package

Create `dto` package:

- `CreateProductRequest`
- `ProductResponse`

### Step 3 — Annotate + map

On request fields use `@NotBlank`, `@Positive` (for price), `@Size` as needed.  
In service: map request → entity → save → map entity → response.

### Step 4 — Controller uses DTO only

Replace `@RequestBody Product product` with `@Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request`.  
Return `ProductResponse`, not the entity.

### Step 5 — Break it on purpose (Postman)

Send invalid JSON:

```json
{ "name": "", "price": -5 }
```

**Expected:** request fails validation (400). Controller method should **not** reach service save logic.

Send a valid body → 200/201 + response without internal-only fields.

***

## Nested objects & lists (quick)

If DTO contains another object:

```java
public record AddressDto(
    @NotBlank String city,
    @NotBlank String zip
) {}

public record CreateOrderRequest(
    @NotNull @Valid AddressDto shippingAddress,
    @NotEmpty List<@NotNull Long> productIds
) {}
```

`@Valid` on the nested field tells Spring to validate inside that object too.

***

## Short map to keep

```text
Entity  = DB shape (internal)
DTO     = API shape (public)
@Valid  = "check annotations before method runs"
starter-validation = brings Hibernate Validator
```
